insight.title: Your Head Is Older Than Your Feet
insight.subtitle: Time passes at different speeds across your own body.
insight.notificationHook: Your head ages faster than your feet

sections.text: Gravity slows down time. Right now, your head is aging slightly faster than your feet simply because it sits further away from the center of the Earth.
The closer you are to a massive object, the slower time passes. Because Earth’s gravity pulls harder on your feet, time moves fractionally slower at your ankles than at your forehead.
This is not just theoretical. Modern atomic clocks can detect this time gap across a height difference of just a few inches, proving time stretches across your physical frame.
You are living through time at different speeds at once.

audioBrief.script:
Welcome to your Sift Daily Briefing. Here is a calm look at everything that matters in the world today.

First up, a recent attack on a vessel near a key maritime strait has thrown the status of diplomatic talks between the United States and Iran into uncertainty. Beyond the immediate conflict, any sustained disruption along this vital shipping corridor could soon drive up global fuel prices for drivers and businesses everywhere.

Meanwhile, the American government has started refunding one hundred billion dollars collected from import tariffs that were ruled illegal. This massive payout means affected businesses across the country may finally recover vital cash after years of paying heavy duties, while courts continue to put tighter checks on executive trade power.

In economic news, India's central bank has chosen to keep its main interest rate unchanged, citing moderate core inflation. For millions of borrowers across the country, this decision keeps loan costs and monthly payments steady, offering a moment of predictability as emerging economies balance growth with inflation risks.

Next, Donald Trump has claimed that foreign influence from China is actively fueling local opposition to artificial intelligence data centers across the United States. If these tensions slow down construction, everyday communities could see delays in essential digital infrastructure upgrades, turning local development projects into a broader geopolitical battleground.

Over in Eastern Europe, Romania has used explosives to blast through river rocks, diverting drought-hit Danube water directly toward a vital nuclear power plant. The dramatic action aims to prevent widespread power outages for local residents, highlighting how severe climate shocks are putting global energy systems to the test.

Switching to public health, the high-profile movement known as Make America Healthy Again is beginning to reshape national wellness priorities in the United States. As policy shifts toward chronic disease prevention, consumers may soon see significant updates to everyday food ingredients and official health guidelines.

In agricultural developments, scientists have created a new, climate-resilient chickpea variety designed to thrive in extremely dry conditions. This seed innovation offers real hope to farmers across southern Africa, helping them protect their crop yields and maintain food supplies during prolonged droughts.

Turning to Ukraine, severe shortages of defense missiles have exposed critical vulnerabilities in the country's air defenses. With fewer interceptors available to block attacks, civilian areas and vital infrastructure face an elevated risk from incoming strikes, underscoring the massive ammunition demands of modern conflict.

In China, the government has unexpectedly issued new tax regulations targeting wealth stored in offshore trusts, sending shockwaves through the country's super-rich. Wealthy investors are now scrambling to sell off assets to settle their tax bills, as global governments work harder to collect revenue from overseas accounts.

Meanwhile, Turkey has introduced draft legislation designed to safely reintegrate former militant combatants back into local communities. If successful, this push for lasting peace could reduce violent conflict and bring much-needed economic stability and security to long-troubled border regions.

Heading to Southeast Asia, a major Indonesian telecommunications firm is seeking a two billion dollar loan to finance advanced computer chips. If secured, the funding will allow local consumers to gain faster access to cutting-edge digital services as the region rapidly expands its technology capabilities.

And finally, Britain is streamlining its stock market regulations in an effort to encourage more companies to list in London. The simplified rules should make it easier for domestic businesses to raise capital, as major financial centers around the world compete to attract new investment.

Before we finish, here is a pleasant thought to end your day on. Science tells us that time actually moves a tiny fraction faster the further you are from the Earth's center of gravity. That means your head is technically a little bit older than your feet. It is a subtle, fascinating reminder that the universe works in quiet ways.

That is your Sift Daily Briefing for today. Have a peaceful day ahead.
